headline: Three midlife risks are linked to dementia

sources.title: Avoiding These 3 Things in Midlife Is Linked to 13 More Dementia-Free Years
3 things to avoid in middle age could mean 13 more years without dementia, study finds
Avoiding 3 risk factors in midlife could add 13 dementia-free years

chunks.text: A long American study {{took in}} 12,409 adults who {{started off}} with [[no sign of]] [[dementia]]. Researchers {{kept track of}} them for about 26 years, and the results were published in the journal Neurology on August 5. The work asked a simple question: how much does health in [[midlife]] change what happens later? It looked at three [[risk factors]]: [[high blood pressure]], [[diabetes]] and [[smoking]].

chunks.text: Adults who had none of the three in middle age {{went on}} to live about 30 years without dementia after the study began. Adults who had all three [[managed]] about 17. The [[gap]] {{adds up to}} roughly 13 years. People with all three were also about 2.7 [[times more likely]] to [[develop]] dementia [[at some point]]. The same [[pattern]] {{came through}} for men and women, with only small differences.

chunks.text: The three factors were measured together, so the study cannot {{single out}} which one matters most. It also cannot {{tell apart}} a real [[cause]] from a [[coincidence]]. This is [[observational]] work: it watched what happened to people who already smoked or already had [[raised]] blood pressure. Money, education and [[genes]] shape health [[as well]], and they may {{make up}} part of the gap.

chunks.text: The numbers are real, but they are not a promise. Nobody can say that if you {{steer clear of}} cigarettes today, or {{cut out}} sugar, or {{get into}} walking, your own dementia will be {{pushed back}} [[by]] 13 years. What the study does show is that doctors already treat these three conditions in [[middle age]], and the same conditions are linked to dementia [[decades]] later. The [[funders]] were the National Institutes of Health.

mainIdea.s: A 26-year study found that adults with no high blood pressure, diabetes or smoking lived about 13 more years without dementia. It only watched people, so the gap may not be a direct cause.
mainIdea.why: Adults with none of the three risks lived about 30 years without dementia, and those with all three lived about 17. The study calls this gap observational, not a proven cause.

mainIdea.s: Doctors say quitting smoking or treating blood pressure today will push back a person's dementia risk by 13 years. The study proves these three habits directly cause the illness later in life.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article says nobody can promise that one person's own risk will be pushed back by 13 years. This is observational work, not proof of a direct cause.

mainIdea.s: A separate study this year found older adults who followed a Mediterranean diet showed slower memory loss over five years. Researchers say the diet may also lower the risk of heart disease.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a different study on diet and memory loss, not about the midlife risks and dementia study.
